gardens-by-the-bay.desc: A 101-hectare garden on reclaimed land beside Marina Bay. The Supertree Grove and outdoor gardens are free; the Flower Dome and Cloud Forest are cooled conservatories with their own tickets.
gardens-by-the-bay.title: Gardens by the Bay: Supertrees, Domes and Free Gardens
gardens-by-the-bay.meta: Plan a day at Gardens by the Bay: the free Supertree Grove and Heritage Gardens, Flower Dome and Cloud Forest, Garden Rhapsody after dark and how to get there.
gardens-by-the-bay.lead: Nowhere sums up Singapore’s idea of a city in a garden better than this 101-hectare park on reclaimed land at Marina Bay.
body: Most visitors stay in Bay South Garden, the largest of the three gardens, which opened in 2012 and holds the Supertrees and the glasshouses. The outdoor gardens and the Supertree Grove are free. The Heritage Gardens tell the island’s story through plants: an Indian Garden with the sacred banyan, a Chinese Garden of rocks, water and pines, a Malay Garden with a kampung house, and a Colonial Garden of nutmeg, cloves, rubber and coffee.

Two cooled conservatories charge admission. The Flower Dome, which Guinness World Records lists as the largest glass greenhouse, gathers plants from the world’s cool-dry regions, including a 1,000-year-old olive tree. Next door, the Cloud Forest recreates misty highland forest around a 35-metre indoor waterfall. At dusk the Supertrees, the tallest of them 50 metres high, light up to music in Garden Rhapsody, free to watch.

A good order for a full day: the Cloud Forest at 9 am, before the crowds and in time for the 10 am misting, then the Flower Dome. Sit out the midday heat indoors, explore the Heritage Gardens in the afternoon, climb to the OCBC Skyway or Supertree Observatory at sunset and stay for the 7.45 pm Garden Rhapsody.

marina-bay-sands-skypark.tag: Three towers and a sky deck on top.
marina-bay-sands-skypark.desc: The public Observation Deck on level 56 of Marina Bay Sands’ Tower 3 gives a 360-degree view of the skyline from the SkyPark atop three hotel towers. Go late afternoon and stay into dusk.
marina-bay-sands-skypark.title: Marina Bay Sands SkyPark: The Observation Deck
marina-bay-sands-skypark.meta: Visit the Marina Bay Sands SkyPark Observation Deck on level 56: off-peak and peak sessions, ticket prices, how to enter via Tower 3 and the best time to go.
marina-bay-sands-skypark.lead: Moshe Safdie balanced the SkyPark across three 55-storey towers, and anyone with a ticket can ride up to its public deck on level 56.
body: Marina Bay Sands opened in 2010 above a mall, theatres, a casino and a convention centre. Its rooftop infinity pool is for hotel guests only, but the Observation Deck on level 56 of Tower 3 is open to everyone, with a 360-degree view of the skyline. Below lie the bay, the Gardens and the city skyline, on land and water that was open sea fifty years ago.

Tickets are sold in two sessions. Off-peak runs from 9.30 am to 4.30 pm; peak, from 5 pm to 10 pm, costs a little more and catches the late-afternoon light and the city coming alight. The deck may close in heavy rain or lightning. For a drink with the view, CÉ LA VI on level 57 has its own entrance and charge; a deck ticket does not get you in.

merlion-park.tag: Half lion, half fish, spouting into the bay.
merlion-park.desc: The 8.6-metre Merlion, Singapore’s mascot, spouts water into Marina Bay in front of The Fullerton Hotel, with a small porcelain-inlaid cub behind it. Free to visit; come early to beat the crowds.
merlion-park.title: Merlion Park: Singapore’s Half-Lion, Half-Fish Mascot
merlion-park.meta: Merlion Park on Marina Bay: the story of Singapore’s 8.6-metre mascot, unveiled in 1972 and moved to the bay in 2002, plus its porcelain cub and when to visit.
merlion-park.lead: Half lion, half fish, the Merlion began life as a 1964 tourism logo and now spouts water into Marina Bay from its own pier.
body: Aquarium curator Fraser Brunner drew the original logo: a fish body for Temasek, the old fishing settlement, and a lion head for Singapura. Local sculptor Lim Nang Seng built the statue, 8.6 metres tall and weighing 70 tonnes, and Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew unveiled it on 15 September 1972. For its first three decades it stood at the mouth of the Singapore River.

When the Esplanade Bridge blocked its view, the Merlion moved to a new pier on Marina Bay in 2002, in front of The Fullerton Hotel. Behind it sits a 2-metre cub inlaid with Chinese porcelain. Entry is free, and the 220-metre Jubilee Bridge, opened in 2015, carries you on to the Esplanade and the rest of the waterfront loop.
merlion-park.tip: Cross the 220-metre Jubilee Bridge to the Esplanade and carry on around the 3.5 km bay promenade.

jewel-changi.tag: The Rain Vortex, an indoor waterfall.
jewel-changi.desc: A glass dome at Changi Airport around the Rain Vortex, a 40-metre indoor waterfall, with a forest valley, shops and restaurants. Easy to visit on arrival or before your flight home.
jewel-changi.title: Jewel Changi Airport: The Rain Vortex and Forest Valley
jewel-changi.meta: Jewel Changi Airport: see the 40-metre HSBC Rain Vortex, walk the Forest Valley and catch the free evening light shows, with opening hours and how to reach it.
jewel-changi.lead: In front of Changi’s Terminal 1, a glass dome holds gardens, shops and restaurants, and at its heart water falls 40 metres through seven storeys.
body: Jewel Changi Airport sits in the public area, linked directly to Terminal 1 and a 5–10-minute walk from Terminals 2 and 3. Jewel bills the HSBC Rain Vortex as the world’s tallest indoor waterfall: it plunges 40 metres from an oculus in the roof and flows daily from 10 am to 10 pm. Seeing the waterfall and the gardens around it costs nothing.

Around it rises the Forest Valley, an indoor garden of more than 900 trees and palms and about 60,000 shrubs, open around the clock, with two half-hour walking trails. After dark the falling water becomes a screen for free light-and-music shows at 8 pm and 9 pm, with a 10 pm show on Fridays to Sundays, public holidays and their eves.
Transit passengers must clear immigration to visit. If you are flying out of Changi, budget time for Jewel before check-in.

artscience-museum.tag: The lotus-shaped museum on the bay.
artscience-museum.desc: Moshe Safdie’s lotus-shaped museum at Marina Bay Sands, with changing exhibitions and the long-running teamLab Future World, an immersive digital-art space that suits all ages.
artscience-museum.title: ArtScience Museum: The Lotus on Marina Bay
artscience-museum.meta: ArtScience Museum at Marina Bay Sands: Moshe Safdie’s lotus-shaped building, teamLab Future World, opening hours, ticket prices and getting there.
artscience-museum.lead: Shaped like a lotus in bloom, Moshe Safdie’s white museum rises from the edge of Marina Bay at the end of the Helix Bridge.
body: Opened in 2011 at Marina Bay Sands, the ArtScience Museum gives each of its frond-like petals a gallery, and rainwater from the roof is channelled down through the atrium. Exhibitions change through the year, but the long-running teamLab Future World, an immersive digital-art space, suits all ages; its Sketch Aquarium lets children design sea creatures that then swim on screen.

The museum sits at the ArtScience end of the 280-metre Helix Bridge, whose LED-lit double spiral of steel carries the waterfront promenade across the bay. Being under cover, it makes a good rainy-day choice, and it pairs easily with The Shoppes at Marina Bay Sands and the free Spectra show on the Event Plaza in the evening.

ocbc-skyway.desc: A 128-metre walkway 22 metres above the ground, strung between the Supertrees at Gardens by the Bay, with views over the Supertree Grove and Marina Bay.
ocbc-skyway.title: OCBC Skyway: Walk Among the Supertrees
ocbc-skyway.meta: Walk the OCBC Skyway at Gardens by the Bay, 128 metres long and 22 metres up among the Supertrees: hours, tickets, maintenance days and the best time to go.
ocbc-skyway.lead: Suspended between two Supertrees, the Skyway lifts you 22 metres above the Supertree Grove, level with the planting panels on their trunks.
body: The Supertrees are vertical gardens built around reinforced concrete cores, their living skins carrying more than 162,900 plants of over 200 species and varieties, from bromeliads and orchids to ferns. Twelve stand in the free Supertree Grove, the tallest reaching 50 metres, about 16 storeys. The 128-metre OCBC Skyway is strung between two of them and looks out over the Grove and Marina Bay.

A visit takes about 15 minutes. Admission may be suspended in bad weather, and the Skyway closes for one full day roughly once a month for maintenance, so check the calendar first. For the Gardens’ highest point, the Supertree Observatory at the crown of the tallest Supertree has an open-air rooftop deck, the same hours and the same price.
facts: Bayfront MRT (Circle, Downtown), Exit B, then Dragonfly or Meadow Bridge
ocbc-skyway.tip: Go in the late afternoon for softer light and lower temperatures.

garden-rhapsody.tag: The Supertrees lit up after dark.
garden-rhapsody.desc: A free light-and-music show at the Supertree Grove at Gardens by the Bay, held twice every evening, at 7.45 pm and 8.45 pm. Lie back beneath the trees and look up.
garden-rhapsody.title: Garden Rhapsody: The Supertree Light Show
garden-rhapsody.meta: Garden Rhapsody at Gardens by the Bay: the free Supertree light-and-music show at 7.45 pm and 8.45 pm nightly, where to watch and how to add Spectra afterwards.
garden-rhapsody.lead: Twice a night the Supertree Grove lights up in time to music, and the best seat is the ground beneath the trees.
body: Garden Rhapsody plays at 7.45 pm and 8.45 pm every evening, a free light-and-sound show played through 68 separate speakers placed around the Grove. Lie back on the paving or find a bench beneath the Supertrees, look up and let the canopies pulse overhead. Themes change about monthly, and the Supertree lights switch off at 11.30 pm. There is no ticket and no booking.

Arrive by 7.30 pm for a spot under the trees; a small mat helps. After the 7.45 pm show, walk across to Marina Bay Sands for Spectra at 9 pm and you have seen both of the bay’s free shows in one evening. From 27 November 2026 to 3 January 2027 the show becomes a Christmas Special, and ticketed events can bring admission charges to the Grove.
facts: Arrive by 7.30 pm for a spot under the trees
garden-rhapsody.tip: On Saturdays, Sundays and Mondays the Borealis light-and-sound installation also plays in the Grove from 8 pm to 8.30 pm; check the Gardens’ website.

singapore-flyer.desc: A 165-metre observation wheel at Marina Centre. One rotation in its glass capsules takes about half an hour, with the whole Marina Bay skyline laid out below.
singapore-flyer.title: Singapore Flyer: The 165-Metre Wheel at Marina Bay
singapore-flyer.meta: Ride the Singapore Flyer, the 165-metre observation wheel at Marina Bay: about 30 minutes a rotation, 28 capsules, opening hours and the nearest MRT station.
singapore-flyer.lead: The Singapore Flyer turns slowly enough that you barely feel it move, while the whole Marina Bay skyline unrolls below.
body: Opened to the public on 1 March 2008, the Flyer stands 165 metres high on a wheel 150 metres across. Its 28 capsules each carry up to 28 people, and one rotation takes about 30 minutes, long enough to take in the bay, the towers and the waterfront at leisure. It runs from 10 am to 10 pm, so you can ride by day or after dark.

The wheel stands at Marina Centre, by Exit A of Promenade MRT. It pairs naturally with a walk along the 3.5 km bay promenade, which links Merlion Park, the Esplanade, the Helix Bridge and Marina Bay Sands; walk early or after 5 pm, when the midday heat has eased. Allow one to two hours for the full loop.

marina-barrage.tag: A green roof between bay and sea.
marina-barrage.desc: The dam across Marina Channel that made the bay a freshwater reservoir. Locals picnic on its free, grassy Green Roof with the skyline in view, and a gallery explains Singapore’s water story.
marina-barrage.title: Marina Barrage: Green Roof, Reservoir and Skyline
marina-barrage.meta: Marina Barrage: picnic on the free Green Roof, visit the Sustainable Singapore Gallery and see how a dam made Marina Bay a reservoir. Hours and transport.
marina-barrage.lead: Opened on 31 October 2008, the Marina Barrage turned the bay at the city’s door into Singapore’s 15th reservoir, and topped it with a lawn.
body: The barrage dams the 350-metre-wide Marina Channel, making the bay the country’s first reservoir in the city centre, with a 10,000-hectare catchment. It stores rainwater for drinking, relieves flooding by releasing surplus water to the sea and gives the city a calm lake for water sports. Inside, the Sustainable Singapore Gallery explains how the country manages its water; it is closed from 12 to 1 pm and on Tuesdays.

Most people come for the grassy Green Roof, open 24 hours and free, where locals picnic with the skyline in view. The whole site is smoke-free and alcohol is banned, so pack a picnic rather than a bottle. It is reached from Gardens by the Bay MRT on the Thomson-East Coast Line, or by bus 400.

fullerton-hotel.tag: The landmark hotel behind the Merlion.
fullerton-hotel.desc: The hotel on the downtown shore of Marina Bay that stands behind Merlion Park. Start here for the Merlion, the Jubilee Bridge to the Esplanade and the 3.5 km waterfront loop.
fullerton-hotel.title: The Fullerton Hotel: Behind Merlion Park on Marina Bay
fullerton-hotel.meta: The Fullerton Hotel stands behind Merlion Park on the downtown shore of Marina Bay: how to reach it, what is nearby and how to start the 3.5 km waterfront walk.
fullerton-hotel.lead: The Fullerton Hotel faces Marina Bay from the downtown shore, and the Merlion spouts water from its pier directly in front.
body: The Merlion moved to its pier here in 2002 from the mouth of the Singapore River, after the Esplanade Bridge blocked its view, so The Fullerton Hotel now forms the backdrop to Singapore’s best-known statue. The name lives on nearby too: the Tan Kim Seng Fountain of 1882 stood in Fullerton Square until it was moved in 1925; today it is a National Monument.

From the hotel’s waterfront, the 220-metre Jubilee Bridge, opened in 2015, crosses to the Esplanade, and the 3.5 km promenade loops on past the Helix Bridge to Marina Bay Sands. Raffles Place MRT is the nearest station on this side of the bay. Walk early or after 5 pm, when the midday heat has eased.

spectra-show.tag: Lights, water and music by the bay.
spectra-show.desc: A free 15-minute show of fountains, light and mist from the Event Plaza in front of Marina Bay Sands, played over the bay every evening. No booking is needed.
spectra-show.title: Spectra: The Free Light and Water Show at Marina Bay
spectra-show.meta: Spectra at Marina Bay Sands: a free 15-minute light-and-water show over the bay every night. Show times, where to watch and how to pair it with Garden Rhapsody.
spectra-show.lead: Since 2017 Spectra has played over Marina Bay every night: 15 minutes of fountains, light and mist, free and with no booking.
body: The show plays from the Event Plaza at Marina Bay Sands and tells Singapore’s story in four acts. From Sunday to Thursday it runs at 8 pm and 9 pm; on Fridays and Saturdays there is a third show at 10 pm. Watch from the waterfront by the plaza, and arrive early if you want a spot right by the water.

Marina Bay puts on two free shows every night, and your only cost is the walk between them. See Garden Rhapsody at the Supertree Grove at 7.45 pm, then walk back to Marina Bay Sands for Spectra at 9 pm. Afterwards, stroll the bay as the skyline lights up. Shows may be cancelled in bad weather or replaced by seasonal specials.
facts: Sun–Thu 8 pm and 9 pm; Fri–Sat 8, 9 and 10 pm

marina-bay-promenade.tag: A night walk around the bay.
marina-bay-promenade.desc: A walking loop of about 3.5 km around Marina Bay that links Merlion Park, the Esplanade, the Helix Bridge and Marina Bay Sands. Allow one to two hours; best at dusk.
marina-bay-promenade.title: Marina Bay Waterfront: The 3.5 km Promenade Loop
marina-bay-promenade.meta: Walk the 3.5 km Marina Bay waterfront promenade past the Merlion, the Esplanade, the Helix Bridge and Marina Bay Sands, with timings, MRT stops and free shows.
marina-bay-promenade.lead: Fifty years ago this was open sea; now a 3.5 km promenade loops past a water-spouting Merlion, a sky park on three towers and an arts centre nicknamed the Durian.
body: Marina Bay is reclaimed land, and the freshwater reservoir at its centre did not exist before 2008. The waterfront promenade opened in 2010 and links every major sight around the bay: Merlion Park, the Jubilee Bridge to the Esplanade, the 280-metre Helix Bridge with its double spiral of steel, and the ArtScience Museum and Marina Bay Sands on the far shore.

Allow one to two hours, and walk early or after 5 pm to avoid the midday heat. Dusk is the moment to be here: the Helix Bridge glows, and the bay stages two free shows, Garden Rhapsody at 7.45 pm and Spectra at 9 pm. As of October 2026 Anderson Bridge is closed, so cross from the Civic District by Cavenagh or Jubilee Bridge.

chinatown.desc: Restored shophouse streets where a Tang-style Buddhist temple, Sri Mariamman, Singapore’s first Hindu temple, and an 1830s mosque stand minutes apart, with two great hawker centres close by.
chinatown.title: Chinatown Singapore: Temples, Shophouses and Hawkers
chinatown.meta: Explore Chinatown: three faiths on South Bridge Road, restored shophouse streets, the Chinatown Heritage Centre and two of Singapore’s great hawker centres.
chinatown.lead: In 1823 Raffles set aside the land south of the Singapore River as the “Chinese Campong”; two centuries on, it rewards anyone who walks it slowly.
body: Chinatown’s Malay name, Kreta Ayer, means “water cart”, after the bullock carts that hauled well water. About 1,000 Chinese lived south of the river in 1821; by 1900 there were some 164,000. The quarter was gazetted for conservation on 7 July 1989, in four parts: Telok Ayer, Kreta Ayer, Tanjong Pagar and Bukit Pasoh. Its shophouse streets are among the finest the Urban Redevelopment Authority has conserved.

On South Bridge Road a Tang-style Buddhist temple, the island’s first Hindu temple and an 1830s mosque stand a few minutes apart. Nearby, the Chinatown Heritage Centre recreates the cramped rooms of 1950s tenants, and lunch means Maxwell Food Centre or Chinatown Complex. South and west, Duxton Hill and Keong Saik Road trade in restaurants and bars.

maxwell-food-centre.desc: Chinatown’s most famous hawker centre, home of Tian Tian Hainanese Chicken Rice, a Michelin Bib Gourmand. Go before 11.30 am or after 2 pm to miss the office lunch crowd.
maxwell-food-centre.title: Maxwell Food Centre: Chicken Rice in Chinatown
maxwell-food-centre.meta: Maxwell Food Centre in Chinatown: home of Tian Tian Hainanese Chicken Rice, a Michelin Bib Gourmand, plus what else to order, when to go and how it works.
maxwell-food-centre.lead: Maxwell is Chinatown’s most famous hawker centre, and the queue at its best-known chicken-rice stall can stretch right out of the building.
body: Maxwell began as a market, opened in 1929, and was one of the post-war sites where the Social Welfare Department served cheap meals to the poor. It became a food centre in 1987, when street hawkers were moved in. Its star is Tian Tian Hainanese Chicken Rice (#01-10/11), which holds a Bib Gourmand in the 2026 MICHELIN Guide Singapore; it is closed on Mondays and takes cash only.

Beyond the chicken rice, look for oyster cake and rojak. As at every hawker centre, find a seat first at busy times, order and pay at the stall, fetch drinks from the drinks stall and return your tray when you finish: tray return has been the law since 2021. Carry small notes, as many popular stalls take cash only.
maxwell-food-centre.tip: Tian Tian closes on Mondays and takes cash only; arrive before 11.30 am or after 2 pm to beat the queue.

lau-pa-sat.desc: A Victorian cast-iron market hall of 1894 in the financial district, open 24 hours. After dark, satay grills fill neighbouring Boon Tat Street for Satay Street.
lau-pa-sat.title: Lau Pa Sat: Satay Street and a Victorian Market Hall
lau-pa-sat.meta: Lau Pa Sat, the former Telok Ayer Market: an octagonal Victorian cast-iron hall of 1894, open 24 hours, with the satay grills of Boon Tat Street after dark.
lau-pa-sat.lead: At lunchtime the office workers of Raffles Place stream towards Lau Pa Sat; after dark, the satay smoke takes over the street outside.
body: The former Telok Ayer Market was built between 1890 and 1894. Municipal engineer James MacRitchie kept the octagonal plan of the 1833 market and dressed it in Victorian cast iron from Walter MacFarlane & Co. of Glasgow. It has been a National Monument since 28 June 1973, the date Singapore’s first monuments were protected. Dismantled in 1986 for MRT tunnelling, it was reassembled in 1989.

The hall is open 24 hours. In the evening, satay grills fill neighbouring Boon Tat Street: Satay Street runs on weekdays from 7 pm to 3 am and at weekends from 3 pm to 3 am. Lau Pa Sat is not on NEA’s list of hawker centres, but you order at the stalls and share tables in the same way.

little-india.desc: Garland stalls, goldsmiths and temples along Serangoon Road, with Tekka Centre for biryani, the Indian Heritage Centre and the 24-hour Mustafa Centre. Most vivid in the weeks before Deepavali.
little-india.title: Little India: Serangoon Road, Temples and Tekka Centre
little-india.meta: Explore Little India: Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple, biryani at Tekka Centre, the Indian Heritage Centre, 24-hour Mustafa Centre and Deepavali on Serangoon Road.
little-india.lead: Along Serangoon Road, garland stalls and goldsmiths fill the shophouse arcades and the gopuram of Sri Veeramakaliamman rises over the traffic.
body: In the 1820s the British set up lime pits and brick kilns along Serangoon Road, and the Indians who worked there called the area Soonambu Kambam, “Village of Lime” in Tamil. Cattle came next, and Kandang Kerbau, the “buffalo enclosure”, grew up west of the road. Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple, dedicated to a fierce form of Kali, began as a shrine raised by lime-pit workers as early as 1855.

Start at the Indian Heritage Centre on Campbell Lane, whose 440-plus artefacts tell the story of Singapore’s Indian and South Asian communities. Then eat at Tekka Centre, whose market dates from 1915, for biryani and tandoor naan, or sit down to a South Indian banana-leaf meal. Mustafa Centre, open 24 hours, sells everything from gold and spices to suitcases.
Little India is at its most vivid in the weeks before Deepavali, when Serangoon Road is strung with lights and bazaars sell saris, bangles and snacks. In 2027 Deepavali falls on Thursday 28 October.

kampong-glam.tag: The golden domes of Masjid Sultan.
kampong-glam.desc: The historic Malay and Muslim quarter around Masjid Sultan, with textile shops on Arab Street, the murals and boutiques of Haji Lane and the restored Malay Heritage Centre.
kampong-glam.title: Kampong Glam: Masjid Sultan, Arab Street and Haji Lane
kampong-glam.meta: Explore Kampong Glam: visit Masjid Sultan, the Malay Heritage Centre in the old istana, Arab Street’s textile shops and Haji Lane, with dress codes and hours.
kampong-glam.lead: The golden domes of Masjid Sultan crown Kampong Glam, where Sultan Hussein’s household once lived alongside Arab, Bugis and Javanese traders.
body: Kampong Glam probably takes its name from the gelam tree, whose bark was used for sails and awnings. The 1822 town plan set land aside here for the Arab community, and the quarter was gazetted for conservation on 7 July 1989. Bussorah Street, heart of the old Kampong Kaji, or Pilgrim Village, where hajj pilgrims lodged while waiting for ships, leads straight to the mosque.

Masjid Sultan’s present building, by Denis Santry of Swan & Maclaren, was finished in 1932; a band of glass bottle ends, donated by poorer worshippers, rings the base of each dome. Nearby, the Malay Heritage Centre reopened in the Istana Kampong Gelam on 25 April 2026. Arab Street keeps its textile shops, and Haji Lane its boutiques, bars and murals.

haji-lane.desc: Reputedly Singapore’s narrowest street, just over 4 metres wide in parts, this Kampong Glam lane is packed with independent boutiques, small bars and wall murals.
haji-lane.title: Haji Lane: Murals, Boutiques and Bars in Kampong Glam
haji-lane.meta: Haji Lane in Kampong Glam: reputedly Singapore’s narrowest street, packed with boutiques, bars and murals, a short walk from Masjid Sultan and Bugis MRT.
haji-lane.lead: Reputedly Singapore’s narrowest street, just over 4 metres wide in parts, Haji Lane squeezes boutiques, bars and wall murals into one slim corner of Kampong Glam.
body: The lane runs through Kampong Glam, the historic Malay and Arab quarter gazetted for conservation in 1989. The quarter was long linked to the hajj: in the late 1800s up to 10,000 pilgrims a year passed through Singapore, many lodging on nearby Bussorah Street while they waited for ships. Today Haji Lane is packed with independent boutiques, small bars and wall murals.

Come in the late afternoon and stay into the evening, when Kampong Glam is at its liveliest. Pair the lane with the textile shops of Arab Street, a visit to Masjid Sultan, closed to visitors on Fridays, and the stalls of Bugis Street, a short walk away near Bugis MRT.
haji-lane.tip: Buying from family-run shophouse businesses in Kampong Glam keeps your money in the neighbourhood.

botanic-gardens.desc: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015, with lakes, a patch of original rainforest and the National Orchid Garden. Free to enter; go early before the heat.
botanic-gardens.title: Singapore Botanic Gardens: UNESCO Garden and Orchids
botanic-gardens.meta: Singapore Botanic Gardens, a UNESCO World Heritage Site: Swan Lake, the Rain Forest, the National Orchid Garden, hours, entry prices and the best MRT stops.
botanic-gardens.lead: Founded in 1859 and inscribed in 2015, the Botanic Gardens are the only tropical botanic garden on the World Heritage List, and they open at five in the morning.
body: The Gardens began as a British colonial garden in the English landscape style and grew into an economic garden and research centre. Their great success was Pará rubber: under director Henry Ridley the Gardens tested and promoted the tree, and the crop transformed Southeast Asia. Today the 82 hectares hold 59 Heritage Trees and the Rain Forest, 6.2 hectares of original lowland forest.

Enter at the Tanglin end, near Napier MRT, for the oldest part, with Swan Lake and the Bandstand, or at Bukit Timah, by Botanic Gardens MRT, for the Learning Forest and the Jacob Ballas Children’s Garden. The National Orchid Garden, the only part that charges entry, holds more than 1,500 orchid species and 3,000 hybrids, among them Vanda Miss Joaquim, the national flower.

national-gallery.tag: Art in the old Supreme Court.
national-gallery.desc: Singaporean and Southeast Asian art in the former Supreme Court and City Hall, two national monuments on the Padang, with the Coleman Deck looking out over the field.
national-gallery.title: National Gallery Singapore: Art in the Old Supreme Court
national-gallery.meta: National Gallery Singapore: Southeast Asian and Singaporean art in the former Supreme Court and City Hall. Hours, ticket prices, free tours and getting there.
national-gallery.lead: Two national monuments on the Padang, the former Supreme Court and City Hall, now hold what the gallery calls the world’s largest collection of Singaporean and Southeast Asian art.
body: The Supreme Court building on the Padang dates from 1939 and City Hall from 1926–1929; on 12 September 1945 Lord Mountbatten accepted the Japanese surrender at City Hall. Together they now form National Gallery Singapore. The Singapore Stories galleries need a General Admission ticket, which includes free guided tours, subject to schedule. The UOB Southeast Asia Gallery is closed until late 2027.

Allow two to three hours, and come on a weekday afternoon, when the galleries make a cool refuge from the heat. The free Building Highlights tour needs registration, and the Coleman Deck looks out over the Padang. Odette, one of Singapore’s three three-star restaurants, is inside the building. Children aged six and under go free.

clarke-quay.desc: Restored 19th-century godowns on the Singapore River, reopened as a dining quarter in 1993 and still the city’s party district after dark. Bumboat river cruises board here.
clarke-quay.title: Clarke Quay: Riverside Bars, Clubs and Bumboat Cruises
clarke-quay.meta: Clarke Quay on the Singapore River: restored godowns turned restaurants and bars, Zouk and the clubs, and bumboat cruises past the Merlion into Marina Bay.
clarke-quay.lead: In the 1800s these godowns were cargo docks on a working river; today Clarke Quay is where Singapore goes out at night.
body: Named after Sir Andrew Clarke, the governor who presided over the 1874 Pangkor Treaty, the quay was gazetted for conservation in 1989, and its shophouses and warehouses reopened in November 1993 as a dining quarter. The oldest building, River House, dates from the 1880s, and two restored tongkang lighters, built in 1968 and 1972, recall the river’s working days. Upstream lies the quieter, residential Robertson Quay.

A S$62 million makeover, relaunched in April 2024, has repositioned Clarke Quay as a day-and-night destination, but it still comes alive after dark. It remains home to the long-running club Zouk. Bumboat cruises board at the jetty here for a loop of about 40 minutes past Raffles’ landing site and the Merlion into Marina Bay.

clarke-quay.tip: Drinking in public places, the river steps included, is banned from 10.30 pm to 7 am; buy and drink in a bar instead.

orchard-road.desc: Singapore’s 2.2 km shopping boulevard, lined almost end to end with malls, department stores and hotels from Dhoby Ghaut to Tanglin. Lit up for Christmas from November.
orchard-road.title: Orchard Road: Singapore’s Great Shopping Boulevard
orchard-road.meta: Orchard Road: 2.2 km of malls from Dhoby Ghaut to Tanglin, plus ION Orchard, Peranakan terraces of Emerald Hill, the Christmas light-up and four MRT stations.
orchard-road.lead: Orchard Road was once lined with nutmeg trees; today it runs for 2.2 km as a tree-shaded avenue of malls, department stores and hotels.
body: Nutmeg plantations spread over this valley in the 1830s, alongside orchards and pepper farms, but prices collapsed and by 1860 few estates survived. Retail arrived in 1958, when C.K. Tang opened his Chinese-roofed department store. Today ION Orchard, directly on top of Orchard MRT, is the flagship of the belt, with nearly 300 stores and ION Sky, an observation deck about 218 metres above ground.

Step off the road and older Singapore returns. Emerald Hill, a short walk up from Somerset, keeps Peranakan terraces with glazed tiles and half-height pintu pagar doors, and the Istana, the President’s residence, opens its gates on a few open-house days a year. Browse indoors at midday, walk the pavements in the evening, and come in November or December for the Christmas light-up.

sentosa.desc: Singapore’s resort island of beaches, Universal Studios, the Singapore Oceanarium and Fort Siloso. Walk in free on the Sentosa Boardwalk from VivoCity, or ride the Sentosa Express or the cable car.
sentosa.title: Sentosa: Beaches, Universal Studios and Fort Siloso
sentosa.meta: Plan a day on Sentosa: Universal Studios, the Singapore Oceanarium, Siloso, Palawan and Tanjong beaches, Fort Siloso, and how to get there from VivoCity.
sentosa.lead: Its old Malay name, Pulau Blakang Mati, translates as “Behind Death”; in 1970 it was renamed Sentosa, for tranquillity, and became Singapore’s playground.
body: The island covers some 500 hectares. Universal Studios Singapore fits seven zones, Minion Land among them, into a single day, and the Singapore Oceanarium, opened in July 2025 at three times the size of the old S.E.A. Aquarium, has manta rays and zebra sharks behind a 36-metre-wide panel. Fort Siloso, free to visit, turned its guns inland in February 1942.

The beaches face the Singapore Strait, so every view is framed by ships at anchor. Siloso Beach in the west is the liveliest; Palawan suits families, with a rope bridge to the Southernmost Point of Continental Asia; Tanjong Beach is the quietest. Most visitors start at VivoCity above HarbourFront MRT and walk in free on the Boardwalk or ride the Sentosa Express.

mandai.tag: Open-concept zoo and a night safari.
mandai.desc: The Mandai Wildlife Reserve in the north: Singapore Zoo, the Night Safari after dark, Bird Paradise, River Wonders and Rainforest Wild Adventure. Plan a full day or an evening.
mandai.title: Singapore Zoo and Night Safari: The Mandai Parks
mandai.meta: Visit Mandai: Singapore Zoo, the Night Safari, Bird Paradise, River Wonders and Rainforest Wild Adventure, with hours, prices and the shuttle from Khatib MRT.
mandai.lead: On the northern edge of the Central Catchment’s forests, the Mandai reserve gathers six wildlife attractions, from an open-concept zoo to a park that opens only after dark.
body: Singapore Zoo opened on 27 June 1973 with 272 animals and made its name with open, natural habitats; Mandai calls it the world’s first open-concept zoo. Today it holds more than 4,200 animals from over 300 species. The Night Safari, opened in 1994 as the world’s first nocturnal wildlife park, is home to more than 900 nocturnal animals, seen from a tram and on four walking trails.

The reserve also holds River Wonders, with Singapore’s giant pandas, Bird Paradise and its walk-through aviaries, the two zones of Rainforest Wild Adventure, the newer of which opened in May 2026, and the indoor Exploria. The M2 Khatib Shuttle runs from Khatib MRT every 15–20 minutes, and multi-park passes cover two or more attractions.

southern-ridges.desc: A 10 km chain of hilltop parks from Mount Faber to Kent Ridge, stitched together by footbridges. The highlight is Henderson Waves, 36 metres above Henderson Road. Best in the late afternoon.
southern-ridges.title: Southern Ridges and Henderson Waves: A Hilltop Walk
southern-ridges.meta: Walk the Southern Ridges from Mount Faber to Kent Ridge Park: Henderson Waves, Singapore’s highest pedestrian bridge, Alexandra Arch and when to go.
southern-ridges.lead: Henderson Waves, Singapore’s highest pedestrian bridge, rolls 36 metres above Henderson Road, and the walk to reach it runs along a chain of forested hills.
body: The Southern Ridges trail follows a 10 km chain of hills from Mount Faber through Telok Blangah Hill and HortPark to Kent Ridge Park. Two bridges, officially opened on 10 May 2008, stitch the hills together over busy roads. Henderson Waves is 274 metres long, its seven curved ribs rising above and below the deck to form shaded alcoves where walkers pause to look over the treetops towards the harbour.

Alexandra Arch, an 80-metre bridge shaped like an open fig leaf, leads to the 1.3 km Forest Walk; at Kent Ridge Park a 280-metre canopy boardwalk reaches Reflections at Bukit Chandu, a Second World War museum. The full walk is long, hilly and partly exposed: start early or late, carry water and wear a hat.

pulau-ubin.desc: An island of about 10 square kilometres, ten minutes by bumboat from Changi Point Ferry Terminal, with wooden villages, old quarries, bicycles for hire and the Chek Jawa wetlands.
pulau-ubin.title: Pulau Ubin: Bumboats, Bicycles and Chek Jawa
pulau-ubin.meta: Visit Pulau Ubin: the 10-minute bumboat from Changi Point, bike hire in the village, the Chek Jawa boardwalk and tides, plus bumboat fares and last-boat advice.
pulau-ubin.lead: Ten minutes by bumboat from Changi, Pulau Ubin keeps the rhythm of the old kampung, with wooden villages, old quarries and mangroves.
body: Bumboats cross from Changi Point Ferry Terminal in about ten minutes. There is no timetable: a boat usually leaves once 12 passengers have gathered, from around 6 am to 7 pm. NParks lists the fare as S$4 per person each way, plus S$2 with a bicycle, but boatmen asked S$5 in 2025, so agree the fare before you board. In the main village you can rent a bicycle or hire a van.

Ride to Chek Jawa at the island’s south-eastern tip, about 3 km from the jetty, where sandy and rocky beach, seagrass lagoon, coral rubble, mangrove and coastal forest meet. Boardwalk loops cross the shore and the mangrove, and the 21-metre Jejawi Tower climbs seven storeys. At low tide the flats reveal sea stars, sand dollars and octopuses; watch, too, for oriental pied hornbills.

tiong-bahru.desc: A 1930s estate of streamlined Art Deco flats, nicknamed “aeroplane flats”, where cafés, bookshops and bakeries mix with long-time residents around a market known for Chinese breakfasts.
tiong-bahru.title: Tiong Bahru: Art Deco Flats, Market and Cafés
tiong-bahru.meta: Tiong Bahru: Singapore’s 1930s Art Deco “aeroplane flats”, Bib Gourmand breakfasts at Tiong Bahru Market, cafés and bakeries, and how to walk the estate.
tiong-bahru.lead: Tiong Bahru means “new cemetery”, a mix of Hokkien and Malay, but its 1930s Art Deco flats now house cafés, bookshops and bakeries alongside long-time residents.
body: The Singapore Improvement Trust completed more than 780 flats here between 1936 and 1941. Architect Alfred G. Church gave the walk-ups streamlined Art Deco lines, and locals nicknamed them “aeroplane flats”. The Urban Redevelopment Authority conserved 20 blocks in 2003. Block 55, at Tiong Bahru Road and Tiong Poh Road, was the first block built in the estate, one of Singapore’s oldest residential neighbourhoods.

Tiong Bahru Market opened in 1951 as Seng Poh Road Market and was rebuilt in 2004–2006. A wet market fills the ground floor; upstairs, 85 cooked-food stalls are at their best at breakfast, with chwee kueh rice cakes, chee cheong fun and yam cake, plus Bib Gourmand stalls for pig’s organ soup and chicken rice. Go early, then walk the estate before the heat builds.

joo-chiat.desc: Colourful Peranakan shophouses, especially on Koon Seng Road, plus Katong laksa, old-school bakeries and Peranakan restaurants along East Coast Road. Come hungry and walk slowly.
joo-chiat.title: Joo Chiat and Katong: Peranakan Shophouses and Laksa
joo-chiat.meta: Joo Chiat and Katong: the pastel Peranakan terraces of Koon Seng Road, Katong laksa, old-school bakeries on East Coast Road and Singapore’s first Heritage Town.
joo-chiat.lead: East of the city the skyline softens, and in Joo Chiat the Peranakan shophouse reaches full volume: pastel façades, carved timber and glazed tiles.
body: Joo Chiat takes its name from Chew Joo Chiat (1857–1926), a migrant from China who bought so much land here that he was known as the “King of Katong”. Peranakan families settled in the early 1900s and built many of the shophouses that survive today. URA gazetted 518 Joo Chiat buildings for conservation in 1991, and in 2011 Joo Chiat became Singapore’s first Heritage Town.

Koon Seng Road, its two- and three-storey terraces built mostly in the 1920s and 1930s, is the most photographed street in the east; Everitt Road and Joo Chiat Place are worth a look too. Then eat: East Coast Road is known for coconut-rich laksa, Peranakan restaurants and old bakeries such as Chin Mee Chin, famed for its kaya toast.

raffles-hotel.desc: Opened in 1887 by the Sarkies brothers and a National Monument since 1987, Raffles is where the Singapore Sling was created in 1915. The Long Bar takes walk-ins only.
raffles-hotel.title: Raffles Hotel Singapore: Home of the Singapore Sling
raffles-hotel.meta: Raffles Hotel, opened in 1887: its history, the Long Bar where the Singapore Sling was created in 1915, the peanut-shell ritual, hours and visiting tips.
raffles-hotel.lead: The Armenian Sarkies brothers opened Raffles as a ten-room hotel on 1 December 1887; by 1915 its Long Bar had created the Singapore Sling.
body: Regent Alfred John Bidwell of Swan & Maclaren designed the main building that followed in 1899, and the hotel became a National Monument in 1987. After a S$160-million restoration it reopened on 16 September 1991. Joseph Conrad, Rudyard Kipling and Noël Coward are honoured in the Writer’s Bar. The hotel stands on Beach Road in the Civic District, a short walk from City Hall and Esplanade MRT.

In 1915 Raffles bartender Ngiam Tong Boon created the Singapore Sling at the Long Bar, a cocktail designed to look like fruit juice so that women could drink it in public. The other ritual is the peanuts: guests brush the shells onto the floor, a custom traced to Malayan plantation owners who drank here at weekends in the early 1900s.

esplanade.tag: The spiky domes on the bay.
esplanade.desc: The arts centre nicknamed the Durian for its spiky twin domes, with free shows most evenings, weekend performances on the outdoor stage by the water and a free Roof Terrace with bay views.
esplanade.title: Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay: The Durian on the Bay
esplanade.meta: Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay: free daily performances, the outdoor theatre by the water, the free Roof Terrace, Makansutra Gluttons Bay and how to get there.
esplanade.lead: More than 7,000 triangular aluminium sunshades cover the twin domes of the Esplanade, which is why Singapore calls it the Durian.
body: Esplanade – Theatres on the Bay opened on 12 October 2002, designed by DP Architects with Michael Wilford & Partners. Inside are a 1,600-seat Concert Hall and a 2,000-seat Theatre. It is also one of the few arts centres in the world with free programmes every day: concerts, dance and community shows on the Concourse, mostly in the evenings. The building is open from 8 am to 11.30 pm daily.

At weekends free performances play at the DBS Foundation Outdoor Theatre, with Marina Bay as the backdrop. Take the lift from Esplanade Mall to the free Roof Terrace on level 4 for the view across to Marina Bay Sands, then eat at Makansutra Gluttons Bay, whose hawker stalls open from 4 pm (3 pm on Sundays) until 11 pm or later.

fort-canning.tag: The old royal hill above the city.
fort-canning.desc: Bukit Larangan, the Forbidden Hill, is now a free 18-hectare park above the Civic District, with 14th-century finds, a Spice Garden recalling Raffles’ first botanic garden and a wartime bunker.
fort-canning.title: Fort Canning Park: Singapore’s Forbidden Hill
fort-canning.meta: Fort Canning Park: from 14th-century Malay kings to Raffles’ first botanic garden, a colonial fort and the 1942 surrender bunker. Free and open 24 hours.
fort-canning.lead: Local Malays held this hill to be the abode of former kings, and called it Bukit Larangan, the Forbidden Hill.
body: Excavations show the hill has been inhabited on and off since the 14th century, when its residents were mostly affluent Malays. Chinese coins and pottery have been found, and in 1928 workers dug up a set of Javanese-style gold jewellery. A kramat on the hill is believed to be the tomb of the last of the kings, and in 1819 local Malays told the British that a royal palace had once stood here.

By 1822 Raffles had a bungalow on the hill and had laid out Singapore’s first botanic garden. A fort, completed in 1861, was mostly demolished by 1926. In 1942 Lieutenant-General Percival decided in a bunker here to surrender Singapore. Today the 18-hectare park is free and open 24 hours, with shady paths and a Spice Garden.

fort-canning.tip: Look for the Spice Garden, planted with turmeric, nutmeg and allspice, a nod to Raffles’ original garden.

asian-civilisations-museum.tag: Asia’s art and trade by the river.
asian-civilisations-museum.desc: Singapore’s museum of the cultures of Asia and the trade links that tied them to the port, on the Singapore River at Empress Place. Open late on Fridays.
asian-civilisations-museum.title: Asian Civilisations Museum: Asia’s Cultures by the River
asian-civilisations-museum.meta: Asian Civilisations Museum at Empress Place: the cultures and trade links of Asia, the Sacred Caves exhibition, hours, Friday late nights and nearest MRT.
asian-civilisations-museum.lead: On the riverbank at Empress Place, the Asian Civilisations Museum tells the story of Asia’s cultures and the trade that tied them to Singapore’s port.
body: The Singapore River curls past Victoria Theatre and the museum towards the bay. Raffles stepped ashore in 1819 near today’s Cavenagh Bridge, the river’s oldest crossing, and for 150 years the river was the engine of the port, crammed with lighters and lined with godowns. The ACM, Singapore’s museum of the cultures of Asia, tells the story of the trade links that tied them to it.

As of October 2026 the special exhibition Sacred Caves: Dunhuang, Buddhism, and the Silk Road is ticketed separately. The museum opens daily from 10 am to 7 pm, and until 9 pm on Fridays; admission ends 30 minutes before closing. Like the other Civic District museums, it makes a good air-conditioned refuge on a thundery afternoon.

peranakan-museum.desc: A museum on Armenian Street about the Peranakan, the Straits-born communities of mixed Chinese, Malay, Indian and other descent, with galleries on origins, family and community life, and fashion.
peranakan-museum.title: Peranakan Museum: Straits-Born Culture on Armenian Street
peranakan-museum.meta: The Peranakan Museum on Armenian Street: galleries on Origins, Family and Community Life and Fashion, hours, tourist prices and late openings on Fridays.
peranakan-museum.lead: On Armenian Street, the Peranakan Museum tells the story of the Straits-born communities of mixed Chinese, Malay, Indian and other descent.
body: The Baba-Nyonya descend from early Chinese settlers in the region and blend Chinese and Malay culture; look for Baba Malay, a creole with many Hokkien words that is now endangered, and hand-beaded slippers called kasot manek. The museum arranges this world around three themes: Origins, Family and Community Life, and Fashion. Peranakan families built many of the shophouses that survive in Joo Chiat, so the museum makes a good primer before a trip east.

Make a meal of it. True Blue Cuisine, a Peranakan dining room on the same street with a 2026 Bib Gourmand, serves the classics, including ayam buah keluak, chicken cooked with the black buah keluak nut. The museum stays open until 9 pm on Fridays, which suits an after-dinner visit, and it is a good choice for a rainy afternoon.

buddha-tooth-relic-temple.desc: A crimson Buddhist temple completed in 2007 in the style of the Tang dynasty, with a relic stupa made with 320 kg of gold and a rooftop prayer wheel. Free; cover shoulders and knees.
buddha-tooth-relic-temple.title: Buddha Tooth Relic Temple: Tang-Style Temple in Chinatown
buddha-tooth-relic-temple.meta: Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum in Chinatown: the relic in its gold stupa, the rooftop prayer wheel, free entry, hours and the dress code to follow.
buddha-tooth-relic-temple.lead: Completed in 2007 at a cost of S$75 million, this crimson temple on South Bridge Road borrows from Tang dynasty architecture and is laid out as a Buddhist mandala.
body: Buddhists venerate the temple’s relic as the Buddha’s left canine, recovered from his funeral pyre at Kushinagar. It rests in a stupa made with 320 kg of gold, which you can view on the fourth floor. On the roof, a pagoda holds a giant Vairocana prayer wheel. The temple and its museum are free to visit, with all floors open daily from 9 am to 5 pm.

It stands on South Bridge Road a few minutes from the Sri Mariamman Temple and Masjid Jamae: three faiths on one street. This is a working place of worship first, so dress for the dress code rather than the heat, and note that meat and pets may not be brought inside. Vesak Day, on 20 May in 2027, is celebrated at Buddhist temples islandwide.

buddha-tooth-relic-temple.tip: Cover shoulders and knees: bare backs, off-shoulder tops, shorts and mini-skirts are not allowed.

thian-hock-keng.tag: A temple to Mazu on the old shoreline.
thian-hock-keng.desc: Built in 1839–1842 by Hokkien immigrants for Mazu, Goddess of the Seas, on Telok Ayer Street, where the shore once ran and new arrivals gave thanks for a safe voyage. Free to visit.
thian-hock-keng.title: Thian Hock Keng: The Temple of Heavenly Happiness
thian-hock-keng.meta: Thian Hock Keng on Telok Ayer Street: a Hokkien temple to Mazu built 1839–1842 and a National Monument since 1973. Hours, history and a walk to Ann Siang Hill.
thian-hock-keng.lead: Telok Ayer Street once ran along the shore, and here early immigrants stepping ashore gave thanks to Mazu for a safe voyage.
body: Hokkien immigrants built Thian Hock Keng, the Temple of Heavenly Happiness, on what was then the shore between 1839 and 1842, dedicating it to Mazu, Goddess of the Seas, with every building material shipped from China. Tan Tock Seng was the largest donor. Chongwen Ge, Singapore’s first Chinese school, stood beside the temple, and the two were gazetted together as a National Monument in 1973.

A restoration from 1998 to 2000 won an honourable mention in the 2001 UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Awards. The shoreline itself, Telok Ayer Basin, has long since been reclaimed. The temple is free to visit and open daily from 7.30 am to 5.30 pm, close to Telok Ayer MRT, and fits easily into a morning among Chinatown’s temples.
facts: 158 Telok Ayer Street; Telok Ayer MRT
thian-hock-keng.tip: Walk on to Ann Siang Hill Park, reached from 78 Club Street.

chinatown-complex.tag: Hundreds of stalls under one roof.
chinatown-complex.desc: Singapore’s largest market and hawker centre, built in 1981 for the last of Chinatown’s street hawkers, with around 700 stalls. See the wet market, then head upstairs for claypot rice.
chinatown-complex.title: Chinatown Complex Food Centre: 700 Stalls in Chinatown
chinatown-complex.meta: Chinatown Complex Market & Food Centre: Singapore’s largest hawker centre, with about 700 stalls above a wet market. Claypot rice, Bib Gourmand picks and tips.
chinatown-complex.lead: Built in 1981 for the last of Chinatown’s street hawkers, Chinatown Complex is Singapore’s largest market and hawker centre, with around 700 stalls.
body: The complex was built to resettle some 300 street hawkers from Smith, Trengganu, Pagoda and Temple streets; after a 2008 upgrade it had more than 700 stalls. The wet market fills the floor below, at its best in the morning, and the food centre is on the second floor. Upstairs, look for claypot rice, yong tau foo, popiah and satay.

Lian He Ben Ji Claypot (#02-198/199) takes 20 to 45 minutes per pot, so order first and find a table while you wait. Xiu Ji Ikan Bilis Yong Tau Fu (#02-87/88) joined the Bib Gourmand list in 2026. Many popular stalls take cash only, so carry small notes, and return your tray when you finish.

Morning for the market; lunch upstairs

east-coast-park.desc: A 13 km seafront park of beach, casuarina shade and cycle track facing ships anchored in the Singapore Strait, with bike and skate rental and East Coast Lagoon Food Village for dinner.
east-coast-park.title: East Coast Park: Beaches, Cycling and Barbecues
east-coast-park.meta: East Coast Park: 13 km of beach and cycle track along the Singapore Strait, with bike rental, barbecue pits, East Coast Lagoon Food Village and when to go.
east-coast-park.lead: Stretching for more than 13 km along the eastern shore, East Coast Park is where Singapore comes to barbecue, cycle and skate at weekends.
body: The 180-hectare park is a long ribbon of beach, casuarina shade and cycle track facing the ships anchored in the Singapore Strait. It is divided into Areas A to H, with landmarks such as the Cyclist Park in Area D and the Xtreme Skatepark in Area F. Bike and skate rental shops line the route, which forms part of the Round Island Route, a planned 150 km loop.

The park is open 24 hours and free, though parking is charged. Ride at sunrise or after 5 pm, when the sea breeze takes the edge off the heat, then eat at East Coast Lagoon Food Village, opened on reclaimed land in 1978. NParks-permitted barbecue pits here are exempt from the ban on public drinking from 10.30 pm to 7 am.
east-coast-park.tip: Spend the morning in Joo Chiat and Katong for a bowl of laksa, then cycle the seafront in the afternoon.

macritchie-treetop-walk.tag: A suspension bridge above the rainforest.
macritchie-treetop-walk.desc: A 250-metre freestanding suspension bridge at canopy level in the Central Catchment Nature Reserve, reached only by forest trails from MacRitchie Reservoir or Windsor Nature Park. Allow three to four hours and carry water.
macritchie-treetop-walk.title: HSBC TreeTop Walk: MacRitchie's Canopy Bridge
macritchie-treetop-walk.meta: Walk the HSBC TreeTop Walk, a 250 m suspension bridge in the forest canopy at MacRitchie: trail routes, opening days, free entry and tips for the heat.
macritchie-treetop-walk.lead: Hung between the two highest points in MacRitchie, the TreeTop Walk puts you level with the rainforest canopy, 25 metres above the forest floor.
body: The HSBC TreeTop Walk is a 250-metre freestanding suspension bridge strung between two hills in the Central Catchment Nature Reserve, the green heart of the island and its main water catchment. From the deck you look straight into the crowns of the trees, 25 metres above the forest floor. The reserve, more than 2,000 hectares of forest around MacRitchie and the other central reservoirs, is also the last refuge in Singapore of Raffles' banded langur, a shy leaf monkey.

There is no short way in. Route 3 is a 10.3 km loop from MacRitchie Reservoir Park; Route 6, about 7 km, starts at Windsor Nature Park on Venus Drive, a 1.2 km walk from Upper Thomson MRT. Allow three to four hours, set off early, before the heat, and keep food out of sight of the macaques that live along the trails.
facts: Route 3 from MacRitchie Reservoir Park (10.3 km loop) or Route 6 from Windsor Nature Park (about 7 km), 1.2 km from Upper Thomson MRT
Tue–Fri 9am–5pm; Sat, Sun and public holidays 8.30am–5pm; last entry 4.45pm; closed Mondays except public holidays
macritchie-treetop-walk.tip: Time your walk to reach the bridge well before the 4.45pm last entry, and carry plenty of water.

bukit-timah.tag: Old rainforest and Singapore's highest hill.
bukit-timah.desc: Trails climb through the island's largest connected area of primary rainforest to the 163-metre summit of Bukit Timah Hill, Singapore's highest point. Go at the 7am opening, when it is coolest.
bukit-timah.title: Bukit Timah Nature Reserve: Singapore's Highest Hill
bukit-timah.meta: Climb through primary rainforest to Bukit Timah Hill, at 163 m Singapore's highest point: opening hours, nearest MRT, free entry and why to go at opening time.
bukit-timah.lead: Inside a reserve protected since 1884, trails climb through one of the last tracts of Singapore's primary lowland rainforest to the island's highest point.
body: Bukit Timah was declared a forest reserve in 1884, after a report by the botanist Nathaniel Cantley the year before, and became an ASEAN Heritage Park in 2011. Its 163 hectares hold the largest connected area of primary rainforest left on the island, original lowland dipterocarp forest mixed with tall secondary growth, rising to the 163-metre summit of Bukit Timah Hill. Summit trails run from 1.2 to 1.9 km.

Listen for birds in the canopy and look down at the streams, home to two freshwater crabs found only in Singapore, among them the Singapore freshwater crab. The reserve is no secret: visitor numbers rose from about 80,000 in 1992 to some 400,000 in 2014. Come at opening time, when it is coolest and before the crowds, and leave pets at home.
facts: Beauty World MRT (Downtown Line); entrance at the end of Hindhede Drive

sungei-buloh.desc: Boardwalks through the largest mangrove forest on mainland Singapore, on the north-west coast, with migrant shorebirds from August to April, otters, monitor lizards and the occasional saltwater crocodile.
sungei-buloh.title: Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve: Mangroves and Migrant Birds
sungei-buloh.meta: Walk the boardwalks of Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve through mangrove and mudflat for migrant birds, otters and monitor lizards: hours, bus and safety tips.
sungei-buloh.lead: On Singapore's north-west coast, boardwalks cross mangrove and mudflat where migrant waders rest, otters hunt and the occasional saltwater crocodile appears on the bank.
body: Sungei Buloh opened as a nature park on 6 December 1993, became a nature reserve in 2002 and, in 2003, Singapore's first ASEAN Heritage Park. Its 202 hectares, extended in 2014, protect the largest mangrove forest on mainland Singapore. The reserve is recognised as internationally important for migratory birds on the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, and migrant waders rest here on their way south between August and April.

Paths and boardwalks lead across mudflats and around ponds. Climb the 18-metre Aerie Tower, and look for the rare lesser adjutant and great-billed heron, monitor lizards on the banks and the resident otters: in 1998 a pair of smooth-coated otters settled here, and the species has since spread across the island. Saltwater crocodiles are occasionally seen, so stay on the boardwalks.
facts: Bus 925 (Mon–Sat) or 925M (Sun and public holidays) from Kranji MRT; 60 Kranji Way
sungei-buloh.tip: Stay on the boardwalks and never approach a crocodile; cycling is not allowed in the reserve.

haw-par-villa.tag: A park of Chinese myths in statues.
haw-par-villa.desc: An 8.5-hectare garden of painted sculptures and dioramas from Chinese legend, built in 1937 by the Tiger Balm brothers and famous for its Ten Courts of Hell. The park grounds are free.
haw-par-villa.title: Haw Par Villa: The Tiger Balm Garden of Chinese Myth
haw-par-villa.meta: Haw Par Villa, the Tiger Balm brothers' 1937 garden of Chinese legend, and the Ten Courts of Hell at Hell's Museum: opening hours, prices, MRT and closures.
haw-par-villa.lead: Built by the Tiger Balm brothers in 1937, Haw Par Villa lines its paths with painted figures from Chinese legend and keeps Singapore's most gruesome dioramas.
body: In 1937 Aw Boon Haw built a villa and garden here for his brother Aw Boon Par; the pair had made a fortune with the pain-relieving ointment known as Tiger Balm. The Japanese occupied the villa during the war and it was later vandalised, but the 8.5-hectare garden of sculptures survived. The Singapore Tourism Board took over in 1988 and ran it for about a decade as a paid theme park, Haw Par Villa Dragon World.

Today the park describes itself as Singapore's oldest theme park and the last Asian cultural park of its kind in the world. Its famous dioramas of the Ten Courts of Hell sit inside Hell's Museum, opened on 28 October 2021, which sets them beside the ways cultures across the world have imagined the afterlife. The sins and punishments are shown in vivid, sometimes explicit, detail, and the museum does not recommend them for children under nine.

Parts of the park have been closed for maintenance since 8 December 2025, until further notice. Come on a weekday morning, before the heat, and ride the Circle Line on to Kent Ridge for a walk on the Southern Ridges.

dempsey-hill.desc: Former British army barracks on an old nutmeg estate, a short ride from the Botanic Gardens, revived since 2006 as Tanglin Village, with its barrack blocks turned into restaurants and bars.
dempsey-hill.title: Dempsey Hill: Dining in Tanglin's Old Army Barracks
dempsey-hill.meta: Dempsey Hill, a nutmeg estate turned British army barracks turned dining quarter near the Botanic Gardens, home of Michelin-starred Candlenut. History and tips.
dempsey-hill.lead: A short ride from the Botanic Gardens' Tanglin gate, Dempsey's old barrack blocks have swapped soldiers for diners, with restaurants and bars where troops once mustered.
body: Dempsey began as Mount Harriet, a nutmeg estate co-owned in the 1850s by Colonial Treasurer William Willans and the merchant Hoo Ah Kay, known as Whampoa. The British military bought it in 1860 and built Tanglin Barracks. Under the Japanese Occupation, British and Australian troops assembled here before marching to internment at Changi, a story told today at the Changi Chapel and Museum.

Singapore took the barracks over in 1971, and from 1972 to 1989 they housed the Ministry of Defence headquarters and the Central Manpower Base. Since 2006 the Singapore Land Authority has revived the area as Tanglin Village, in three clusters, Dempsey, Minden and Loewen, with the old barrack blocks turned into restaurants and bars.

The best-known table is Candlenut, at 17A Dempsey Road, whose Peranakan cooking, built on the chef's family recipes, has held a Michelin star in every Singapore edition since 2016. Share dishes à la carte or choose the tasting menu, which changes every three months.
facts: Short taxi ride from the Botanic Gardens' Tanglin gate or Orchard Road
Dinner, after a day at the Botanic Gardens
dempsey-hill.tip: Book ahead for dinner at Candlenut, the Michelin-starred Peranakan restaurant on Dempsey Road.

holland-village.tag: Cafés and bars with a village feel.
holland-village.desc: A crescent of shophouses and small malls around Lorong Liput and Lorong Mambong, west of the Botanic Gardens, where expatriates settled from the 1990s and the bars followed. It has its own Circle Line station.
holland-village.title: Holland Village: Shophouse Bars West of Orchard
holland-village.meta: Holland Village, or Holland V, a crescent of shophouses, small malls and bars around Lorong Mambong with its own Circle Line station: history and getting there.
holland-village.lead: West of the Botanic Gardens, Holland V gathers its shophouses and small malls around two short lanes, a neighbourhood that fills up in the evenings.
body: Holland V, as Singaporeans call it, is a crescent of shophouses and small malls around Lorong Liput and Lorong Mambong. Holland Road is said to be named after Hugh Holland, an architect and early resident. Next door, Chip Bee Gardens was built as married quarters for the British military; from the 1990s expatriates moved in, and the bars followed. With Dempsey, it is where the evenings beyond Orchard Road are spent.

The newest arrival is One Holland Village, which opened in December 2023. Holland Village has its own station on the Circle Line, and Dempsey and the Botanic Gardens are a short taxi ride away, so the gardens by day and Holland V or Dempsey by night make an easy pairing for an unhurried day in the west of the city centre.

jurong-lake-gardens.desc: Singapore's third national garden and its first in the heartlands: 90 hectares around Jurong Lake, with restored Chinese and Japanese Gardens, lakeside walks and the Clusia Cove water playground.
jurong-lake-gardens.title: Jurong Lake Gardens: Singapore's National Garden in the West
jurong-lake-gardens.meta: Jurong Lake Gardens: 90 ha of lakeside planting with the Chinese and Japanese Gardens, Clusia Cove water play and Forest Ramble. MRT stations, hours and tips.
jurong-lake-gardens.lead: Singapore's third national garden spreads 90 hectares around Jurong Lake, from pagodas and a teahouse to a water playground whose flows mimic the tides.
body: Jurong Lake Gardens is Singapore's third national garden and its first in the heartlands. Lakeside Garden opened in 2019, and the rejuvenated Chinese and Japanese Gardens, first built in the mid-1970s, reopened on 8 September 2024, completing the gardens. In the Chinese Garden the old Cloud Pagoda, Twin Pagoda, Stoneboat and Bonsai Garden stand beside new features such as Cascading Creek; the Japanese Garden adds a Water Lily Garden, Sunken Garden and Teahouse.

Lakeside is the family end. Clusia Cove is a three-hectare water playground whose flows mimic the tides, and Forest Ramble, at 2.3 hectares the largest nature playgarden in the heartlands, has 13 adventure stations inspired by local wildlife. Rasau Walk follows the lake edge, and the gardens are the western start of the 36 km Coast-to-Coast Trail to Coney Island Park.

old-airport-road.desc: One of Singapore's earliest purpose-built hawker centres, completed in 1973, with more than 160 cooked-food stalls. Come for Hokkien mee, fried kway teow and kway chap, five minutes' walk from Dakota MRT.
old-airport-road.title: Old Airport Road Food Centre: Hawker Classics Since 1973
old-airport-road.meta: Old Airport Road Food Centre, completed in 1973, has 160+ cooked-food stalls, including Bib Gourmand kway teow and kway chap: what to eat and how to get there.
old-airport-road.lead: Completed in 1973, Old Airport Road is one of Singapore's earliest purpose-built hawker centres, and some of its cooks have spent decades perfecting a single dish.
body: Independent Singapore chose to house its street hawkers rather than banish them, moving them from 1971 into purpose-built centres with running water and proper waste disposal. Old Airport Road Food Centre, completed in 1973 at Block 51 Old Airport Road, is one of the earliest, with more than 160 cooked-food stalls under one roof. Each stall is its own business, with its own number, prices, hours and rest day.

Nam Sing Hokkien Fried Mee (#01-32) has cooked one dish since 1960, and Lao Fu Zi Fried Kway Teow and To-Ricos Kway Chap hold Bib Gourmands. There are no waiters or bills: find a seat, walk the aisles, read the signboards and join the queue that looks right. Share a few plates and you taste several communities in one sitting.
facts: Dakota MRT (Circle Line), about 5 minutes' walk; Blk 51 Old Airport Road
Hokkien mee, fried kway teow, kway chap

newton-food-centre.tag: Open-air hawker centre for late dinners.
newton-food-centre.desc: Singapore's first garden-style hawker centre, opened in 1971 near Orchard and busiest after dark, known for barbecue seafood, oyster omelette and carrot cake. Check prices before you order seafood.
newton-food-centre.title: Newton Food Centre: Singapore's Garden-Style Hawker Centre
newton-food-centre.meta: Newton Food Centre, Singapore's first garden-style hawker centre, opened in 1971: barbecue seafood, Bib Gourmand stalls, the MRT exit and the best time to go.
newton-food-centre.lead: Opened in 1971 as Singapore's first hawker centre with a garden setting, Newton Food Centre comes into its own after dark, when the seafood stalls are busiest.
body: Newton Food Centre opened in 1971, Singapore's first hawker centre with a garden setting, in the year the country began moving its street hawkers into purpose-built centres. Upgraded in 2006, it stands at 500 Clemenceau Avenue North, close to Orchard, and is busiest at night. The classic orders are barbecue seafood, oyster omelette and fried carrot cake, the radish cake fried with egg.

Alliance Seafood (#01-27, Bib Gourmand) cooks seafood to order with barbecue, sambal, black pepper or salted egg yolk, and its cereal butter prawns are a highlight. Heng (#01-28) is the stop for carrot cake, and Hup Kee Fried Oyster Omelette (#01-73) joined the Bib Gourmand list in 2026. Return your tray when you finish: since 2021 it has been the law.

Barbecue seafood, oyster omelette, carrot cake

geylang-serai.desc: The traditional heart of Malay Singapore, which comes alive around Geylang Serai Market and, above all, during Ramadan, when a vast bazaar and street lights fill the district before Hari Raya.
geylang-serai.title: Geylang Serai: The Heart of Malay Singapore
geylang-serai.meta: Geylang Serai, the traditional heart of Malay Singapore: its history, Geylang Serai Market and the Ramadan bazaar and street light-up before Hari Raya Puasa.
geylang-serai.lead: Named after the lemongrass once grown here, Geylang Serai is where the Malay east still shops, feasts and celebrates, loudest of all in the nights before Hari Raya.
body: Serai is Malay for lemongrass, once grown widely on the Alsagoff family's Perseverance Estate; Geylang may come from kilang, a mill, perhaps for coconut oil. Orang Laut, the sea nomads, settled by the Geylang River in the 1840s, and in 1910 Singapore's first tramline had its eastern terminus here. From the 1950s the population became predominantly Malay, and Infopedia calls the district the Malay emporium of Singapore.

Redevelopment from the early 1980s brought HDB blocks, but life still gathers around Geylang Serai Market, opened in 1964 and rebuilt in 2009. During Ramadan the streets are lit up, a tradition begun in 1985, and a vast bazaar draws people of every background for snacks, kueh from home cooks and the evening breaking of the fast.

coney-island.tag: A wild little island in the north-east.
coney-island.desc: An 81-hectare rustic island park at Punggol, with five themed beaches, an estuary and more than 80 bird species recorded. There is no parking on the island, so come by MRT to Punggol Coast.
coney-island.title: Coney Island Park: Punggol's Rustic Island Park
coney-island.meta: Coney Island Park in Punggol: 81 ha of rustic beaches and estuary, 80+ bird species, hours, the nearest MRT, entrances and tips on sandflies and wild boars.
coney-island.lead: Off the north-east coast at Punggol, Coney Island Park has been left rustic: five themed beaches, an estuary and more than 80 bird species recorded.
body: Coney Island Park covers 81 hectares at Punggol, in the north-east, and has been kept as a rustic island park rather than a manicured one. Its five themed beaches and estuary draw birdlife, with more than 80 species recorded. There are two entrances, one near Punggol Point at the west end and the other near Lorong Halus Wetland at the east, and the park is open from 7am to 7pm.

The island marks the eastern end of the 36 km Coast-to-Coast Trail, which crosses Singapore from Jurong Lake Gardens via the Lornie Nature Corridor; NParks' free NEAR app helps you walk it in sections. There is no parking on the island, so come by MRT. Wild boars live here: keep clear of them, and do not feed the monkeys.
facts: Punggol Coast MRT; entrances near Punggol Point (West) and Lorong Halus Wetland (East)
coney-island.tip: Wear long trousers and covered shoes against sandflies, and carry water.

bishan-amk-park.tag: A canal turned back into a river.
bishan-amk-park.desc: A 62-hectare heartland park where the Kallang River, once a concrete canal, now meanders between wildflower banks. More than 90 bird species have been recorded, and it is famous for its otters.
bishan-amk-park.title: Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park: The River Set Free
bishan-amk-park.meta: Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park, where the Kallang River was freed from a concrete canal: 62 ha of wildflower banks, otters and 90+ bird species, open 24 hours.
bishan-amk-park.lead: In Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park the Kallang River has been let out of its concrete canal, and now winds between wildflower banks through a park more than 3 km long.
body: The Kallang River once ran in a concrete canal along the edge of this heartland park. Today it meanders between wildflower banks through 62 hectares, more than 3 km from end to end, and wildlife has followed: more than 90 bird species, including the purple heron, and over 30 butterfly species have been recorded. Climb Recycle Hill for the view, or walk round the pond of more than 2 hectares.

The park is also otter country. The Bishan family of smooth-coated otters, at its peak 14 strong and the largest group recorded, became national celebrities and in 2016 was chosen as an icon of the nation's 51st birthday. Watch them from a distance and give them space: otters have bitten people who crowded them.
facts: Bright Hill MRT, about 5 minutes' walk; Bishan MRT nearby
bishan-amk-park.tip: Use the Ang Mo Kio Avenue 1 entrance; the Marymount Road junction entrance has been closed since 2020.

changi-village.desc: A low-rise village at the island's eastern tip, with a food centre where nasi lemak is the classic order, a coastal boardwalk and the ferry terminal for bumboats to Pulau Ubin.
changi-village.title: Changi Village: Nasi Lemak, Boardwalk and Bumboats
changi-village.meta: Changi Village at Singapore's eastern tip: nasi lemak at the food centre, the Changi Point Coastal Walk and bumboats to Pulau Ubin. Buses, fares and tips.
changi-village.lead: At the island's eastern tip, Changi Village feels a world away from the city: low buildings, a food centre, a boardwalk and bumboats waiting for Pulau Ubin.
body: Changi Village is a cluster of low buildings, a bus terminal, a food centre and the Changi Point Ferry Terminal at 51 Lorong Bekukong. At the food centre, nasi lemak, coconut rice with sambal and fried fish or chicken, is the classic order. Buses 2, 29, 59 and 109 run to Changi Village Bus Terminal, and Changi Airport is next door, so the village makes an easy add-on if you are flying in or out.

From the ferry terminal, the Changi Point Coastal Walk hugs the shore for about 2.2 km, past bumboats heading for the offshore islands, along the beach and around the cliffs; allow about 45 minutes. Bumboats cross to Pulau Ubin in about ten minutes. There is no timetable: a boat usually leaves once 12 passengers have gathered, from around 6am to 7pm.
NParks lists the bumboat fare at S$4 per person each way, plus S$2 with a bicycle, but boatmen have asked for more, so agree the fare before you board.
facts: Buses 2, 29, 59 or 109 to Changi Village Bus Terminal
About 10 minutes; around 6am–7pm; S$4 each way (NParks)

sri-mariamman-temple.desc: Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, founded by 1827 on South Bridge Road in Chinatown, with a five-tier gopuram crowded with painted deities. Visit during the morning or evening sessions, and remove your shoes.
sri-mariamman-temple.title: Sri Mariamman Temple: Singapore's Oldest Hindu Temple
sri-mariamman-temple.meta: Sri Mariamman Temple in Chinatown, Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, founded by 1827: its painted gopuram, Theemithi fire-walking, opening hours and etiquette.
sri-mariamman-temple.lead: Behind a five-tier gopuram crowded with painted deities, Sri Mariamman on South Bridge Road has been a place of worship since at least 1827.
body: Singapore's first Hindu temple was founded by Naraina Pillai, a clerk from Penang who came with Raffles in 1819, and a shrine of wood and attap stood here by 1827. Mariamman, the goddess at its heart, is venerated for protection against epidemic disease. The five-tier gopuram over the entrance, crowded with painted deities, was remodelled in 1936, and the temple became a National Monument in 1973.

It stands on South Bridge Road a few minutes from the Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Masjid Jamae, three faiths on a single street. The temple is at its most intense in the week before Deepavali, when devotees walk on hot coals at the Theemithi fire-walking festival; visitors can watch from an elevated gallery in the courtyard.
facts: 244 South Bridge Road, Chinatown; Chinatown MRT (North East and Downtown lines) serves the quarter
Morning prayers; Theemithi in the week before Deepavali (28 October 2027)

masjid-sultan.desc: Kampong Glam's great mosque, finished in 1932 to a design by Denis Santry, its golden domes ringed with glass bottle ends. Visitors are welcome at set hours, Saturday to Thursday; dress modestly.
masjid-sultan.title: Masjid Sultan: Kampong Glam's Golden-Domed Mosque
masjid-sultan.meta: Masjid Sultan, Kampong Glam's golden-domed mosque, completed in 1932: its history, visiting hours, the dress code and etiquette for visitors to the mosque.
masjid-sultan.lead: The golden domes of Masjid Sultan crown Kampong Glam, and around the base of each runs a band of glass bottle ends given by poorer worshippers.
body: A single-storey brick mosque was completed here in 1826, on land set aside under Sultan Hussein's 1824 agreement with the East India Company. Its replacement, designed by the Irish architect Denis Santry of Swan & Maclaren, was formally opened in 1929 while only two-thirds built, and finished in 1932. A band of glass bottle ends, donated by poorer worshippers, rings the base of each golden dome. It became a National Monument on 8 March 1975.

The prayer hall holds 5,000, and visitors may enter it only with a mosque official. The visitors' entrance is Gate 5, facing Bussorah Street, once the heart of Kampong Kaji, the Pilgrim Village, where hajj pilgrims lodged while they waited for ships. Men need sleeved tops and long trousers; women need long sleeves and ankle-length skirts or trousers. Flash-free photography is allowed; video needs approval.
facts: Bugis MRT (East-West and Downtown lines); visitors' entrance at Gate 5, facing Bussorah Street
Visiting Sat–Thu 10am–noon and 2pm–4pm; closed to visitors on Fridays

sri-veeramakaliamman.desc: Little India's temple to Veeramakaliamman, a fierce form of Kali, where Tamil lime-pit workers raised a shrine as early as 1855. Its painted gopuram rises over the traffic of Serangoon Road.
sri-veeramakaliamman.title: Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple: Kali on Serangoon Road
sri-veeramakaliamman.meta: Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple in Little India, a shrine to Kali since about 1855: its history, puja times, Thaipusam, how to get there and temple etiquette.
sri-veeramakaliamman.lead: Over the garland stalls and goldsmiths of Serangoon Road rises the gopuram of Sri Veeramakaliamman, Little India's temple to a fierce form of the goddess Kali.
body: In the 1820s the British set up lime pits and brick kilns along Serangoon Road, and Tamil workers from the lime pits of Kampong Kapor raised a shrine here as early as 1855. It was the first temple in Singapore to Veeramakaliamman, a fierce form of Kali. Bengali labourers built a temple in 1881, and after municipal labourers took over its management it was restored from 1908, with a Kali statue shipped from South India.

Come early in the morning, perhaps after breakfast at Tekka Centre, or at a puja, a prayer time, for bells, lamps and chanting. At Thaipusam, devotees walking the route down Serangoon Road may pause at the temple; watch respectfully, and do not enter temples where devotees are fulfilling their vows.

national-museum.tag: The nation's oldest museum, newly revamped.
national-museum.desc: Singapore's oldest museum, on Stamford Road, whose Singapore History Gallery reopened on 10 October 2026 after its first full revamp, tracing more than 700 years from maritime trade to the global city.
national-museum.title: National Museum of Singapore: 700 Years of History
national-museum.meta: The National Museum of Singapore reopened its Singapore History Gallery in October 2026 after a full revamp: what to see, opening hours, MRT and tickets.
national-museum.lead: Singapore's oldest museum marked its 139th anniversary by reopening its Singapore History Gallery, revamped in full for the first time, on 10 October 2026.
body: The National Museum of Singapore is the nation's oldest museum and the place to see the full national story. Its Singapore History Gallery reopened on 10 October 2026 after its first full revamp, and its seven zones cover more than 700 years, from maritime trade to the global city. Look for the Singapore Stone and the piano on which Zubir Said wrote the national anthem.

The museum stands on Stamford Road, served by Bras Basah and Dhoby Ghaut MRT stations. The Level 2 Life in Singapore galleries reopen fully in early 2027. Citizens and permanent residents enter free; tourists need a ticket, so check the museum's website for current prices. Everything is under cover, which makes the museum one of the best rainy-day choices in the city.

Free for citizens and PRs; tourists ticketed (check the museum's website)
